## Mob chat

Speaker: Andrew Curran, @AndrewCurran_, who writes about AI. Claim date: displayed as September 5, 2026 at 2:26 AM on X. X renders timestamps in the viewer's timezone, so the UTC instant needs confirmation. Collected September 4, 2026 UTC.

Original: x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/209606239244…

### The claim

Curran presents this as a new prediction. He says Anthropic has solved a Millennium Prize Problem, and specifies that "Claude has solved Navier-Stokes." He says the result is out for expert review, and sets himself what he calls a hard deadline: the announcement comes before the IPO.

Source limitation: x.com refuses automated retrieval, so the wording above comes from an indexed copy of the post rather than the live page. Capture an archive and confirm against the original before admission.

### Proposed components

These are three parts of one claim and should be grouped so they cannot earn separate points.

- Substance. Anthropic has a solution to the Clay Institute's Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem. Curran does not say which direction the result runs, global regularity or finite time blowup, and does not say the problem is the 3D incompressible case, though that is the Clay formulation. "Solved" needs an admission definition: a Clay qualifying resolution, a claimed proof released for review, or a partial result described publicly as a solution.

- State. The result is currently under expert review. This is a present tense assertion about a private process. It is likely unfalsifiable from public evidence unless Anthropic or a named reviewer confirms it later, and it should be flagged as such rather than scored on silence.

- Deadline. The announcement lands before Anthropic's IPO. The deadline is event dated and the triggering event is unscheduled and may never occur. Admission needs a convention covering what counts as the IPO, whether an S-1 filing, direct listing, or acquisition triggers resolution, and a backstop calendar date so the record cannot stay open indefinitely.

Classification: ordinary forecast. No numerical probability, no stated stake, no counterparty, no wager acceptance.

### Speaker track record

Curran posts these deliberately as datable predictions, which makes him a good candidate for a standing record. Two earlier ones are resolvable and would give the leaderboard a baseline before this one is scored:

May 20, 2026, that Gemini Pro 3.5 and GPT-5.6 were both finished and both labs wanted to ship, and that they were held back for safety testing under a forthcoming executive order: x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/205719456579…

June 30, 2026, that a significant architecture breakthrough in memory efficiency came from an OpenAI spinout other than SSI, with an announcement expected soon: x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/207207689373…

### Context, not corroboration

Terence Tao published a piece treating Navier-Stokes as a worked example on September 3, 2026, summarized at teorth.github.io/tao-web/ai-views.html , and repliers to Curran reference a Tao thread plus same day rumors. The timing may explain why the post appeared. It is not evidence that the claim is true, and reviewers should not let proximity stand in for confirmation.

### Requested before this leaves submissions

Verify the original timestamp and archive the post, fix the definition of a solved Millennium problem, and write the IPO deadline convention including a backstop date.

### Shane Legg: 50% chance of AGI by 2028

Speaker: Shane Legg, Google DeepMind cofounder and Chief AGI Scientist. Claim date: October 26, 2023. Primary interview and transcript: dwarkesh.com/p/shane-legg

> And so, yeah, I think there's a 50% chance that we have AGI by 2028.

Legg defines AGI in the interview as "a machine that can do the sorts of cognitive things that people can typically do, possibly more." He proposes a broad range of tests against human performance, including efforts to find cognitive tasks on which the machine still falls short.

Speaker probability: 0.50. Stated horizon: by 2028. A year-end cutoff and exact timezone would be admission conventions. The source definition and breadth of testing must be retained when choosing resolution evidence. He explicitly says he would not be surprised if AGI arrives later. Classification: ordinary probabilistic forecast.
